en: When they urgently gathered the people,
A curtain with a silken weft,
When they drew it across this side,
Gold by the pood, bright red gold,
When they took it as the bridal attendants’ fee,
Seventy young wives and ninety girls
Stood as go-betweens.
When they went to put her to bed,
Hanging misfortune about his neck,
As a maiden, with Manas
She refused to lie in his arms.
We saw the trouble that luckless one caused:
Drawing out her dagger,
Before Manas had lain down,
She struck and split his forearm.
“She has grievously humiliated me,” he said.
“Before I even lay down, this girl
Stabbed my forearm open,” he said.
He found a quarrel in the festivities;
Laying Bukhara waste,
Khan Manas raided it six times.
For the people of this Bukhara,
Because of that arrogant, luckless one,
The wide world became narrow.
These people of Bukhara,
For a donkey’s offspring,
For even its foal, then longed in vain.
As a married woman, this fierce one
Upset customs and ruined the people;
When this woman was a girl,
She shook the world and ruined the people.
The wretch who stabbed Manas,
Would she refrain from stabbing us?
That crafty, luckless one who did that to Manas—
Would she have pity on us?
“Let the fierce woman be the hero,” he said.
“If to the river Kara-Dengiz
We do not drive them all the way,
May our seven forefathers be unbelievers,” he said.
“Like a bare horse-tethering rail,
May we pass away with nothing.
All the way to the place you named,
If we do not drive your horse,
If we do not obey your words,
May we die as unbelievers.”
Licking deadly poison,
Swearing an oath on his life,
He chewed white wheat flour;
He swore upon the Holy Quran;
He made his promise firm;
Then he made a pledge that could cost a man his life.
Having made his promise firm,
Old Eshen drove the horses away.
The horses were driven to their place,
And had long since arrived.
Taitoru was entered as an omen
By Kanykei, the prince’s wife.
Let us leave this here;
Ismail, the khan of Bukhara,
Kanykei’s brother of the same nest—
Let us begin our tale with him.
That Ismail of whom we speak,
Of the same nest as Kanykei,
Not merely of one nest, but born in succession,
Children of one father,
Camel calves of one mother.
Ill-fated Ismail,
Staying in Bukhara, heard the news:
“Kanykei has gone astray;
Staying in Bukhara, carried away,
She raced her horse,” he heard.
“A widow, yet she grows so excited—
Would that the earth swallowed her!
‘I shall race my horse,’ she raves,
Taking a shortcut by Ichke-Zhol,
Her one horse of sixty mature years,
The unbeliever leads it, saying, ‘I shall race it.’
God has struck that shameless one!
There she stands, saying, ‘I shall race my horse.’
God has struck that fool!
If she does this, the raging woman will bring no good;
If so, she will not leave us unharmed.
The unbeliever, excited though a widow,
Raving, ‘I shall race my horse’—
Can anyone be so shameless?
Running wild while in mourning,
Can an unbeliever be like this?
Eagerly crying, ‘I shall race my horse,’
Making straight for her wayward path,
This raging woman, though in mourning,
Leads her Taitoru.
Whose bones are these that ache?
Whose honor has been broken?
Whose honor has departed?
Whose honor has returned?
The unbeliever, excited though a widow,
Raving, ‘I shall race my horse,’
Dresses herself in men’s clothes.
Can anyone be such a fool?
Rejoicing that her husband died,
Taking a shortcut along her crooked road,
She has caused grievous trouble,
Raving, ‘I shall race him,’
Leading her Taitoru.
Or has this raging bitch
Sought a husband among eight khans
And failed to find one?
With her heart turning toward a husband,
Has the bitch come to ruin?”
My noble brother-in-law Manas—
Can one who defiles his bed prosper?
Who sits dishonoring the lord,
This shameless one of such a kind,
Could she ever prosper?
If she keeps dishonoring Manas,
Can a bitch who acts thus prosper?
Fortunate Manas was a lion,
All of those many lands,
He was the hero who set them free.
Who sits dishonoring his spirit,
A woman of this kind,
Could she ever prosper?!
With a support like Temir,
Ismail's elder sister—
Let no one say she raced her horse
And was left behind!
For this shameless woman's sake,
Rather than be mocked by the people,
Unless I send Semetey in fury,
Unless I seize her upon the road,
Have her dragged along the road,
That calamity-bringing bitch,
Unless I seize and split her on the road!”
So spoke Ismail.
Ismail's white palace—
Its door was iron, solid tin.
His majesty far surpassed the people's;
Was he not a khan of great standing?
Anyone who saw Ismail's form was frightened.
He had seven guards,
Human noses and ears
They wore fastened as amulets.
Seventy executioners,
Forty sword-bearing guards—
No person approached;
Not a mite of strength remained in them.
Was not Ismail a khan
Of considerable majesty?
His knees bent to the ground.
A grove of plane trees surrounded it,
A golden throne stood in the middle.
Running up to his throne,
Ismail sent word,
To Semetey first,
And then to all his executioners.
He sounded the drum.
Five times he had his shawm
Cry out with great force.
He struck his kettledrum with a crash,
And sounded his small drum.
When Ismail sent word,
When they heard this news,
Their knees bending,
His wrestlers came running.
Their leaders of ten bobbed in their saddles,
His commanders of fifty hurried:
“What dispute has arisen?” they said.
“Where is an enemy abroad?” they said.
The most skillful of the spearmen,
His marksmen who never missed,
His orators who never faltered,
His learned men, his elders,
All thronging as though an enemy had come,
All his wrestlers
Came and stood there.
Bukhara's khan Ismail
Roared in anger.
“Come here!” he said then,
Calling Semetey.
When Semetey arrived,
The bastard let loose,
Speaking ill of his elder sister Kanykei.
At that time, Semetey
Had not yet worn a cloak upon his shoulders;
Manas, gone to the other world—
He did not yet know he was his father.
Kara-Kyr stretching out—
He did not yet know it as his horse-line.
The grieving woman Kanykei—
He did not yet know she was his mother.
His mother Kanykei,
Hunched like a hunting hound,
He did not yet know how she had trotted.
Fleeing Talas, wandering on foot,
He did not yet know how she had come.
Until the Five Wild Sheep stars set,
Her white breast, slender as a spindle—
He did not yet know he had suckled it.
Kanykei had once come in mourning;
Semetey had come fleeing to Bukhara.
He prospered by plundering their valuables,
The child entered Bukhara and grew up.
He reached manhood and became a hero,
Became the equal of warriors' sons.
Chipped from white steel,
Taken in and raised by Ismail,
He came to Bukhara and matured.
His thoughts were elsewhere.
At that time, Semetey
Was Khan Ismail's son,
Temir Khan's camel-calf.
He had emerged a burning ember.
In mighty Bukhara's city,
No such unruly boy had appeared.
Ismail in Bukhara
Resolved to take hostile action.
Speaking ill of Kanykei,
He now told a remarkable tale:
“Oh, Semetey, my foal,
I heard news from those who came.
Your ill-omened elder sister,
Running wild in her widowhood,
Carried away with the wish to race a horse,
Has sunk into disgrace, I heard!
Rejoicing that her husband died,
That wretch, fierce as ever,
Donned a man's clothes,
Took a shortcut along a broken road,
A horse of sixty mature years,
She leads, saying she will race it.
Unable to manage wearing a dress,
Unable somehow to marry a man,
She went seeking men and stirred up trouble.
She has brought us boundless shame.
Making them say, ‘His sister is a widow,’
My child, she has brought trouble upon us all.
How can we bear to see such conduct?
Having her called a wandering woman,
Rather than be a laughingstock to all,
Let us die instead of living.
Oh, Semetey, my foal,
My river in its valley, my spring,
My little one, gained through mortal anguish,
My soft, gray-speckled falcon,
My gray goshawk, my morning star,
Hey, Semetey, go there and return.
If Taitoru comes in front,
Shouting ‘Manas! Manas!’
Raising the battle cry ‘Manas!’
Drive him here and bring him back.
If Taitoru falls behind,
Seize the bitch
And offer her up as a sacrifice.
Have her dragged along the road
And split her open for the dogs.
Cut off her head and fasten it,
